legend: Toad Zitz has an array of integers, each integer is between 0%%ZSMJ0%% and m−1%%ZSMJ1%% inclusive. The integers are a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ2%%.

In one operation Zitz can choose an integer k%%ZSMJ3%% and k%%ZSMJ4%% indices i1,i2,…,ik%%ZSMJ5%% such that 1≤i1<i2<…<ik≤n%%ZSMJ6%%. He should then change aij%%ZSMJ7%% to ((aij+1)mod%%ZSMJ8%% for each chosen integer i_j%%ZSMJ9%%. The integer m%%ZSMJ10%% is fixed for all operations and indices.
Here x \bmod y%%ZSMJ11%% denotes the remainder of the division of x%%ZSMJ12%% by y%%ZSMJ13%%.
Zitz wants to make his array non-decreasing with the minimum number of such operations. Find this minimum number of operations.
input: The first line contains two integers n%%ZSMJ14%% and m%%ZSMJ15%% (1 \leq n, m \leq 300\,000%%ZSMJ16%%) — the number of integers in the array and the parameter m%%ZSMJ17%%.
The next line contains n%%ZSMJ18%% space-separated integers a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n%%ZSMJ19%% (0 \leq a_i  \lt  m%%ZSMJ20%%) — the given array.
output: Output one integer: the minimum number of described operations Zitz needs to make his array non-decreasing. If no operations required, print 0%%ZSMJ21%%.
It is easy to see that with enough operations Zitz can always make his array non-decreasing.
note: In the first example, the array is already non-decreasing, so the answer is 0%%ZSMJ22%%.
In the second example, you can choose k=2%%ZSMJ23%%, i_1 = 2%%ZSMJ24%%, i_2 = 5%%ZSMJ25%%, the array becomes [0,0,1,3,3]%%ZSMJ26%%. It is non-decreasing, so the answer is 1%%ZSMJ27%%.
